speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, I move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head L of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has been a privilege chairing the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Sustainability and the Environment who have pushed hard for positive changes, a privilege to have seen first-hand the good work done by our dedicated teams at the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE), National Environment Authority (NEA), Singapore Food Agency (SFA) and Public Utilities Board (PUB).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MSE does vital work in safeguarding the food we eat, the water we drink, the environment in which we live, work and play in, our climate and the survival of this planet we call home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know it is rare for me to stand up here for almost a minute already and not ask questions, call for changes and nag for things to be done.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But truly and sincerely, we have seen much progress made in MSE's policies and legislation and I am truly grateful.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many activists are thankful that many of their voices have been heard and our policies, especially on the climate change front, have improved significantly over the years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this Committee of Supply (COS), I look forward to hearing more about the progress from the hard work of our teams again at MSE, NEA, SFA and PUB.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I almost ended this speech without asking for anything, but you know, that is impossible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure Senior Minister of State Amy Khor and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng expect me to talk about second-hand smoke and I shall not disappoint them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have done so well in so many areas except in the area of second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fresh air is as vital as fresh food, fresh water and a healthy planet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I truly and sincerely hope that MSE can put our hearts and minds towards tackling the issue of second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know my GPC colleagues and fellow Members of Parliament will be asking lots more questions about the Ministry's other plans for 2025.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Addressing climate change will assist and ensure Singapore's long-term resilience and sustainability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As a densely-populated island nation with limited resources, strategic urban planning and promoting sustainable practices and core components of an effective climate change strategy is critical.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: How is the Ministry engaging with communities to foster a culture of sustainability and encourage individual actions that contribute to a climate-resilient future?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: And finally, how is the Ministry collaborating with international partners and organisations to share best practices and innovations in building sustainable and climate-resilient cities?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore, as a small and open economy, faces dual pressures, staying competitive amid global decarbonisation efforts while mitigating the adverse impact of climate change.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is not just an economic issue but also a national resilience challenge.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Countries worldwide are tightening carbon regulations and implementing green tariffs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Businesses that fail to adapt risk being left behind.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To remain competitive, Singapore must lead in green innovation and establish itself as a hub for low-carbon technologies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Government to accelerate investments in green industries.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also urge the Government to strengthen our workforce capabilities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must expand SkillsFuture funding for green skills, ensuring our workforce is future-ready.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This includes training in sustainability reporting, carbon trading and climate risk assessment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, I also urge the Government to enhance our carbon pricing strategy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Smaller businesses often struggle with upfront costs for sustainable transformation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A targeted fund could provide upfront co-funding for energy-efficient technologies and green certification.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can work with Association for Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) partners to develop cross-border carbon credit markets and supply chains for green materials.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This positions Singapore as the go-to hub for sustainable trade.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, also to expand expanding the Enterprise Sustainability Programme (ESG).

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I urge that more direct assistance should be provided for the SMEs adopting ESG practices, including tax incentives for sustainability investments.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Climate change is not just an economic challenge.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Rising sea levels, extreme weather and food security concerns demand long-term resilience planning.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must continue expanding local food production and invest in alternative energy sources, like regional renewable imports and nuclear research.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A just transition must ensure that lower-income households are not disproportionately affected by climate policies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Utility rebates and green job opportunities should be integrated into our support measures.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As an island surrounded by seawater, all coasts are at risk of the rising sea level.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on the site-specific studies of our coasts?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most Singaporeans would have heard about the East Coast Plan.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have about 64 islands, of which, seven belong to the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF).

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Measures must be taken to protect their shores as well, as there are implications for our defence planning.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are the mitigating measures planned for the islands for civilian use, such as Sentosa; and industrial use, such as Jurong Island?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our drainage infrastructure has been continuously upgraded to reduce flood-prone areas.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Which areas are expected to benefit from recent works and what are the target dates for their completion?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would MSE share how it is working with building owners and transport operators to prepare for potential floods in high-risk areas?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will MSE engage drivers to bring them onboard flood warning systems?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To improve thermal comfort, our buildings should be built to mitigate the heat effect of our tropical climate.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Glass facades are not suitable for tropical buildings because they absorb excessive solar radiation, leading to overheating indoors.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What new measures will MSE be implementing to improve thermal comfort in public spaces, including hawker centres and community centres?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When temperatures spike, what are the warning signs and warning systems as well as advisories that will be in place to keep the public safe, especially workers, the elderly, students, uniform personnel and residents doing sports?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must act decisively to balance economic competitiveness with climate resilience.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By investing in green industries, supporting businesses and fortifying our society, we can position Singapore as a global leader in sustainable development.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I look forward to MSE's response on how we can sharpen our strategies in these critical areas.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, the road to building a strong commitment to climate change is a long and winding one, with crisscrossing headwinds along the way as some governments wane in the face of challenges, like rising interest rates, economic hiccups, from inflation to business downturn, to name a few.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And you have the new political leadership in the White House, which, again, withdrew its membership from the Paris Agreement adopted in 2015.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Some see climate action as something about declaring dates to achieve net-zero carbon emissions, but there are just too many barriers to overcome.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have seen developing countries being asked to "leapfrog" to renewable energy, but the adoption of renewable energy is not something that can be done with the switch of a button.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It requires a lot of investment and certainly, a strong will to change to clean energy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Besides, many are so used to fossil fuel that they become addicted.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore, according to a report by EcoBusiness, one of Asia Pacific's independent media and business intelligence organisation dedicated to sustainable development, "few firms can confidently say they know how they will be completely negating their greenhouse gas output by 2050 – a feat scientist regard as the best bet to keep global temperatures from rising past 1.5 degrees Celsius and causing extreme climate risks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Experts say it is necessary for firms to stomach such uncertainty and gun for net-zero targets, given the urgency of tackling climate change, though there must be preparation work in resourcing and talent development." May I ask, how can Singapore stay competitive amid global pressures to decarbonise, while also managing the adverse impact of climate change?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How will the Government support our businesses in these areas?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, in warm and sunny Singapore, air conditioning is widely used in homes, offices and shops.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The problem is that our widespread use of air conditioning is actually pushing up external temperatures and contributing to global warming.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Air conditioners exacerbate the urban heat island effect; use hydrofluorocarbons, which are potent greenhouse gases, as refrigerants; and consume high amounts of electricity generated from fossil fuels.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What is the Ministry doing to change the attitudes and behaviours of Singaporeans towards sustainability, so as to reduce the use of air-conditioning in indoor spaces?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, you may take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will have an impact on electricity bills.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With expected higher electricity bills, businesses will be hard hit.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, it is not easy for many companies to change their operations to be more energy efficient.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sunk investment costs in current equipment and tools, lack of expertise knowledge, among other constraints, are major obstacles for them, especially for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the help and supporting measures MSE would offer businesses to increase their energy efficiency?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Utility bills are likely to increase despite lower fuel prices due to higher carbon taxes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we face hotter days and warmer nights, many households are turning to air conditioning and showers to cool themselves down, which result in higher electricity and water bills.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What kind of support will the Ministry provide the households with, to help them manage their energy and water consumption more efficiently?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share about its public education outreach and advisories to motivate and help households adopt more green lifestyle habits and transition to more efficient home appliances?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Chairman, many of us will remember the enthusiasm when Singapore's National Recycling Programme was launched in April 2001.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: NEA rolled out a team of the public waste collectors (PWCs) were licensed to provide recycling bins and recycling collection services to all Housing and Development Board (HDB) estates, as well as private landed properties and condominiums who were opted into the public waste collection scheme.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The 3Rs – Reduce, Reuse and Recycle – form the pillar of NEA's schemes.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: It developed a suite of initiatives as part of Singapore Green Plan and Zero Waste Masterplan.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The aim is to shift attitudes as well as behaviours to make 3Rs the norm for citizens, as well as businesses.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: NEA also continues to study and develop new ways to close the various resource loops.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I note that NEA has been exploring the use of mixed materials from Semakau Landfill, which comprise of incineration ashes and other waste materials, as reclamation fill.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: There is greater awareness now, among households to support this recycling exercise which is commendable.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: There is a greater commitment from individuals to build a sustainability culture by embracing the 3Rs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What are the current challenges facing the recycling industry and how can the Government help the industry and promote more sustainable recycling as a way of life in Singapore?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It was reported that NEA was considering broader forms of packaging waste under the extended producer responsibility scheme.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This is a step in the right direction to achieve Singapore's climate goals.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry share the insights gleaned from the Mandatory Packaging Reporting scheme and how they would impact the extended producer responsibility scheme?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry provide an update on measures to manage the key waste streams, including packaging waste?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This has been a mantra that has been ingrained in me from a young age.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my younger days, I had thought that the 3Rs was the gold standard for sustainable living.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That misinformed fantasy of mine was smashed when I visited one of Singaporeans' favourite travel destinations: Japan.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Japanese families meticulously sort their waste into plastic, paper, metal and glass.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To recycle a soft drink container, one would have to clean and dry the PET bottle to prevent residual contamination, remove paper labels and metal cap, and deposit each item in different recycling bins.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such societal norms have its roots in a worldview that is a deeply reverent of Mother Nature, something Japanese children learn from a young age.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Singapore, our National Recycling Programme aims to make recycling more convenient, but we do face several challenges.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our Blue Bins are a single-stream system where all recyclables are collected.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While this simplifies the process, contamination is a problem, when non-recyclables or items that have yet to be cleaned get thrown in the mix, especially.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some Queenstown residents have also expressed concerns about the limited capacity of recycling bins and the low frequency of collection.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, bins sometimes overflow before scheduled collections, forcing recyclables to be discarded as trash to maintain cleanliness.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore's recycling trucks also lack multiple compartments to keep materials separated.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even if households sort their recyclables, they would still be mixed during collection.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This raises concerns about the effectiveness of the system and begs the question of whether additional investments can and should be made in upgrading infrastructure to support better recycling practices.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What else can the Ministry do to facilitate Singaporeans in truly embracing the 3Rs as a way of life?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More restaurants now charge for plain water and some price bottled water, the same as sugary drinks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This nudges consumers towards sugar laden beverages, increasing the risk of obesity and diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Free or low cost drinking water should be made more widely available across food and beverage (F&B) outlets, shopping malls, hotline, coffee shops and public spaces.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This supports healthier choices and reduces unnecessary costs for consumers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I urge MSE to encourage and work with F&B outlets, coffee shops and malls to provide free, or low cost drinking water as a best practice.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MSE should also promote the culture of carrying reusable water bottles as part of Singapore's sustainability efforts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Refilling reusable bottles cuts down our reliance on single use plastics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By nudging businesses, building owners and the public towards these norms, we can help Singaporeans stay hydrated while making choices that benefit their health, their wallets and the environment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, the need to invest in climate adaptation measures cannot be more pressing.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Ministry provide an update on the progress on coastal protection plans, both on the "Long Island" project and site specific studies, together with any early results?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the progress of PUB's Code of Practice study to develop legislation surrounding coastal protection and how will these measures be appropriately enforced to ensure compliance?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Ministry ensure that coastal protection measures are adequately funded?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond coastal protection measures, our neighbourhoods have been more vulnerable to floods lately, such as in Bukit Timah in December 2024 and Jalan Seaview in January 2025.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Ministry also provide an update on plans to upgrade drainage infrastructure and enhance flood resilience?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How is the Ministry engaging communities to ensure that Singapore continues to be flood ready?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And can there be any tech-enabled solutions to keep Singaporeans apprised of potential flooding in a timely manner?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Chairman, climate change is causing more frequent and extreme rain events, which have led to flash floods in various parts of our island.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: We need to be prepared against floods inland due to rainfall and coastal floods from sea level rise.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: We are experiencing more sudden and heavy rainfalls which leave homeowners and businesses with less time to react, such as putting up protective barriers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Will the Minister share what measures will be implemented to better protect buildings in low-lying areas, buildings with basements and underground Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) stations against floods?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on the plans to upgrade our drainage infrastructure to enhance our flood resilience?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How is the Ministry engaging members of the public to increase their awareness and ensure that Singaporeans are well prepared in the event of floods?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Sadly, today, flash floods after a heavy downpour has become more common.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: And flash floods are occurring not just in Bukit Timah, but also across the island.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: One explanation given is this is due to rapid urbanisation and the other is the unpredictability of heavy downpours, with the torrent of water swiftly filling up our canals and drains.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Whatever the real causes, we should analyse the current flooding patterns and use technology to predict future flooding patterns and recommend solutions to mitigate the impact.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: This will allow for more collaborations between these properties owners to manage their flood risks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: In managing flood prone areas, does solving one area flooding problem result in adjacent areas or downstream flooding of another area?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can the Minister provide an update on plans to upgrade our drainage infrastructure and enhance flood resilience?

text: How is the Ministry engaging communities to ensure that Singapore continues to be flood-ready?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Could the Ministry provide an update on the progress on coastal protection plans and how will the Ministry ensure the coastal protection standards are met?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Chairman, in view of global warming, it is important for Singapore to strengthen our heat resilience.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Our densely populated city-state is also experiencing the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Could the Ministry provide an update on heat resilience plans, in view of rising temperatures in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What measures are being taken to improve the thermal comfort of our public spaces and better protect vulnerable segments of our population and outdoor workers?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The Government had launched the OneMillionTrees movement to plant a million more trees across Singapore by 2030.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Would the Ministry update us on how many trees have been planted to date and whether we are on track to reach our target?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Would the Ministry also share the progress of environmental modelling for new towns and estates to site buildings in ways to optimise wind and air flow?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The residents of three households are affected by the excessive noise and heat from the bakery located on the ground floor.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Back then, I made a representation to NEA and HDB Bedok Branch Office.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Nine years later, in 2023, Mr A, together with two other residents, Mr B and Mr C, came to see me with similar feedback and I escalated the matter to MND.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In October last year, 2024, Mr C returned to see me, citing the situation remains despite the numerous communications with the relevant agencies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: He also told me that his two other neighbours have shifted out.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This time around, I wrote to SFA to seek assistance.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My clarifications are: how often does SFA receive similar feedback in a year?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: What are SFA's requirements for bakeries to operate in a HDB residential block emitting the noise and heat levels resulting from their daily operations?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My proposal is for SFA to consider bakeries to be regulated with adequate noise control measures as well as sufficient ventilation systems, similar to features like those installed for bakeries located at HDB blocks, so as to be more effective in diffusing heat and vapour.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my speech during the Second Reading of the Food Safety and Security Bill in January, I highlighted the crucial role farms play in ensuring Singapore's food security, especially with more frequent extreme weather patterns in future.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should, therefore, equip our farms with effective mitigation measures against climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While high-tech innovations have strengthened our food security, we must also recognise the potential of tried and tested low-tech methods that can enhance the resilience of our agricultural sector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Low-tech agricultural practices rooted in traditional knowledge and ecological principles offer cost-effective and sustainable ways to mitigate the effects of climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many of these techniques have been successfully implemented elsewhere worldwide, and Singapore can benefit by adapting them to suit our land-scarce farmscape.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A good example is the Back Halloween Farm in France, which employs permaculture to create a high use sustainable system on a small land area.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Permaculture mimics natural ecosystem by fostering synergies between crops and animals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This approach includes growing different crops side by side, rotating them accordingly, and designing water channels for natural irrigation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It has proven useful against extreme weather events, despite enduring three consecutive record-breaking dry summers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The farm experienced minimal disruption by interweaving a diverse root network with dense vegetation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The soil retained moisture like a giant sponge, shielding crops from extreme weather.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Moreover, this technique has proven more effective per square metre than conventional mechanised farming, garnering interest from scientific institutions worldwide.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Similarly, our fish farms can incorporate natural solutions like aqua plants to improve climate resilience.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Aqua plants provide shade and cooling, stabilising water temperatures and prevent algae blooms by absorbing excess ammonia while producing oxygen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Importantly, they reduce the risk of hypoxia, oxygen depletion, a significant challenge during Singapore's hotter months when warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While technology remains crucial for precise monitoring and control, aqua plants offer a valuable low-tech complement for fish farms.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, such low-tech solutions are not necessarily low cost.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Permaculture consultations are offered by local companies like GWS and Habitat Collective but require substantial investment in research, adaptation and implementation to be effective at a commercial scale.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The availability of funding for these solutions will provide adequate support for adoption by farmers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In this way, Singapore can build a more resilient and sustainable agricultural sector, better prepared for climate change challenges.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, in today's challenging business climate, rising costs, supply chain disruptions and climate change, our local farms and food businesses need greater support to build resilience and grow sustainably.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How can we enhance financial support, technology adoption and innovation to improve productivity?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Are there further efforts to strengthen our local farm capabilities and help them scale up?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A resilient agri-food sector is key to Singapore's food security and we must continue to do better to support this vital industry.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: However, we have experienced some setbacks, such as reports of vegetable, poultry and fish farms shutting in recent years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: How is the Government supporting local farms, given the challenging business climate and has the Government seen an increment in the take-up rates of productivity grants?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I was glad to see that this is a collaborative effort and thank all involved, as aquaculture is yet another demand on our limited sea space which is highly utilised.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: What regulations are in place to ensure any businesses which set up fish farms in open waters will keep our marine environment clean?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many grants for Singapore's sustainability, sustainable food sector, such as NEA's Closing the Resource Loop Funding Initiative and SFA's Singapore Food Story, appear to prioritise public agencies and Institutes of Higher Learning.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For instance, requiring a principal investigator's H-index and citation count may not be suitable for startups and private enterprises, which often avoid publishing research due to commercial sensitivities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To fully harness Singapore's innovative potential, could the Government refine grants to better support local startups and SMEs at higher technology readiness levels, easing access to funding by reducing complexities or removing the requirement for public sector partners?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: If current grants primarily serve Institutes of Higher Learning and public agencies —

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: — would it consider new funding to help innovative private enterprises scale and contribute to sustainability goals?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More than 10 years ago, in a 2013 publication, a National Heritage Board (NHB) Community Heritage e-resource on wet markets identified the numerous challenges facing wet market stall-owners, such as competition from hypermarkets, changing consumer profiles, unwillingness of children to take over stalls, significant physical labour and long hours.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Despite challenges, some wet markets remain relatively more popular, with Tekka Market and Geylang Serai being good examples.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chair, our hawker centres are our national canteens and provide a wide variety of affordable food to suit more palates and budgets.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We have had many popular hawker centres sited all over Singapore, which have served residents over many years.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Their structures are ageing and some can do well with some upgrading, others may need to be rebuilt to optimise layouts.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since its opening in the 1970s, Marsiling Lane Market and Food Centre has been well patronised by Singaporeans, especially those living in Marsiling and Woodgrove.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In recent years, the surrounding neighbourhood has been transforming rapidly.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The HDB's rejuvenation of Heartland project wrapped up last year.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A new Marsiling Community Club will be in operation from next year, and we are welcoming several new BTOs in the area.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Against this backdrop, Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad and I, as Members of Parliament (MPs) for Marsiling and Woodgrove divisions, respectively, often get asked by residents whether and when the market and hawker centre can get a rejuvenation too.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Rejuvenation would be ideal, especially since the hawker centre is thriving and packed on weekends.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Such rejuvenation ought to, on the one hand, further improve the customer experience for everyone, including younger folks, while keeping food prices and wet market shopping affordable.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the other hand, we would have to consider how these heartland markets are often quiet on weekdays and at night.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Should we then expect hawkers to stay open during those periods?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Shops also face stiff competition from Johor Bahru, which is proximate and convenient for Singaporeans, especially those residing in the north to head to.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How can we make the hawker and wet market experience in Marsiling more attractive, especially with the Rapid Transit System (RTS) coming and worries that business might take a hit?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For a start, we should upgrade all hawker centres to meet the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) Green Mark standards to create a better environment for hawkers and patrons.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We could also set up a hawker agency to manage these centres, encourage hawker entrepreneurship, and boost food and service quality, including healthier options.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That way, our hawker centres and wet markets can thrive.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And we can continue to keep our hawker culture alive.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Many a spirited debate has ensued over which area has the best mee rebus, freshest fruits and tastiest "kopi peng".

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: To that, I would put forward that the answer is in Ang Mo Kio.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: With the inscription of hawker culture in the UNESCO list, hawkers are in the spotlight, but many are growing older and struggling with both cost pressures and legacy challenges as it is not easy to attract and sustain younger players.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: How are we supporting both hawkers and wet market stallholders to remain competitive in the current cost environment?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I am grateful for the Hawker Centre Transformation Programme (HTP), which was helpful in upgrading older markets, such as the Cheng San Market and Cook Food Centre in Ang Mo Kio.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Older hawker centres often have fundamental infrastructure issues which are hard to resolve through regular Repair and Redecoration (R&R) works and persistent challenges such as urban birds, heat and drainage.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: How else can we more comprehensively upgrade our hawker centres to keep them clean and cool for generations to come?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Eric Chua, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Hawker centres provide affordable, good-quality meals and serve as communal spaces where people from all walks of life gather.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Whenever I seek budget-friendly and delicious food, hawker centres are my go-to choice.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: However, while regulations governing our hawker centres today have generally served us well, I would like to ask the Ministry if some rethinking of our rules might be opportune, especially in view of the need to adapt to the changing realities confronting our hawkers today.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: A significant challenge among our hawkers today is their physical self.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Many hawkers are getting on in years and are not as physically able as before.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Many veteran hawkers, who have spent decades perfecting their craft, now find it increasingly difficult to work long hours.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: As a result, many stalls in some hawker centres close by the late afternoon, and this translates to reduced food options and overall foot traffic to these hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: This not only impacts individual stallholders' revenue but also affects the vibrancy and appeal of these centres as our community hubs.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: To be sure, this calls for careful planning: food types sold across the two shifts should ideally be complementary; and infrastructural provisions such as allocated storage areas or spaces for the preparation of food must be redesigned.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: However, should these teething challenges be successfully worked through, such an arrangement would enable different hawkers to operate the same stall at different times of the day, thereby ensuring the continuity of food options for consumers and retaining the vibrancy of our hawker centres for a much longer stretch of the day.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: On a related note, many successful hawkers have built strong brand recognition, with many loyal customers seeking out their food.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: However, the inability to operate beyond two stalls restricts their ability to meet demand.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: However, I understand that some hawkers are still hesitant about doing so.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Regular reviews and recalibration of existing frameworks will ensure that hawker centres remain accessible, sustainable and adaptable to the evolving needs of hawkers and consumers alike.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: By fostering a more flexible and forward-looking approach, we can continue to uphold Singapore's rich hawker heritage while ensuring its long-term viability for future generations.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Mr Eric Chua: Madam, I am Hokkien, and Hokkien mee is one of my favourite hawker food.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: I recently ate my first plate of Hokkien mee that was not cooked by a human hawker.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: My Hokkien mee was cooked by a robot, named Wok AI.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: To my surprise, the Hokkien mee was delicious, just a touch lacking in "wok hei", something that even Chip, the engineer-turned-hawkerpreneur has been working on, and by now, he might already have "cracked the code" to achieve ideal "wok hei".

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: It could also ensure consistency in taste and consumers might even be able to personalise our dishes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Could the Ministry please provide an update on how YOPH has turned out?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: When it comes to public hygiene, the Ministry should continue its focus on particularly these three areas: one, tackling high-rise littering; two, dealing with unhygienic public toilets; and three, reducing waste.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: These steps can cut down the risk of community disease outbreaks from things like rats, pigeons, stray wildlife and mosquitoes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Can the Ministry update us on its plans and efforts in this regard?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: For example, with high-rise littering, how fast does the agency act to set up surveillance cameras when residents say the problems keep popping up?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Could the Ministry boost its resources to speed up deployment and enforcement?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: In November 2024, I attended the Waterloo finale of results of National Survey on toilets in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: It was a project led by the Singapore Management University's Rosie Ching, principal lecturer of statistics, with her 222 undergraduate students from her Statistics X course.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: They conducted on-site surveys to check toilet cleanliness across Singapore's public spaces.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Even with efforts to raise hygiene standard last year, coffee shop toilets were slightly worse than in 2023.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: In my closing address at the event, I shared that public hygiene is something we all share responsibility for.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: It is not just the Government, but operators, cleaners, users, the general public including you and I, can all step up to push for cleaner public toilets.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: I would therefore urge the Government to team up with these passionate students, continue to engage and interview other stakeholders, not just to point out how dirty our public toilets are, but to come up with long-term fixes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: We need an outcome-based approach to make sure all public toilets are functional, clean and hygienic.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Too many toilet facilities that stay under repair for ages leaves people without option.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: The Government could also consider setting up an endowment fund to keep funding efforts to transform toilets, making them clean, safe and barrier free, especially for our ageing population.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I have spoken up so much that Senior Minister of State Amy Khor once said that she is immune to me already.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But on a more serious note, this is a serious issue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It is not about how many people have complained about this issue but quite starkly, about how many people have died.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is not about the luxury of having fresh air to breathe or nice-smelling air.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is a matter of life and death for so many people who depend on us sitting here to protect them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It is time for us to legislate and ban smoking at windows and balconies so that fewer people will die from second-hand smoke.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Can the Ministry give an assessment of whether the Taskforce's recommendations will be considered or implemented?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Coffee shop toilets have been ranked the filthiest consistently for years.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, please take your four cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The Public Toilets Task Force (PTTF) was established in March 2024 to study and recommend ways to improve the cleanliness of public toilets in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Ministry share its views of the recommendations in its recently released report?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Will the stakeholders, such as coffeeshop operators, owners and cleaning companies, be able to go onboard the new cleaning framework?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Although Singapore is still considered a clean and green city, problems of littering still remain.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: In fact, like other Members, I personally received many complaints from my residents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: As many had commented before, Singapore is not so much a clean city per se, but a cleaned one, with many hardworking cleaners picking up after litterbugs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How will the Ministry tackle this problem and reduce the cases of littering?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Parks, beaches and public toilets are some of the cleanliness hotspots in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How will the Ministry address the hygiene problems at these locations as well as at others, such as parts of Chinatown and certain hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Will customised solutions be required to address the different causes and contributing factors to low standards of cleanliness at these sites?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The Project Wolbachia has been a great success.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Eric Chua, take your two cuts together, please.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: I fully support the project and its continued implementation.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: However, for some residents, especially those whose homes are on lower floors, living with the constant release of male Wolbachia mosquitoes has caused some inconveniences.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: While I usually share NEA's advisory that they do not have to exercise restraint in swatting mosquitoes they come across, few found solace in my advice.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: One resident with sensitive skin even purportedly developed rashes because of the increased mosquito population.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Would the MSE and NEA then be able to help ameliorate the disamenities that residents face with the project's implementation?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: In Queenstown, residents have raised concerns regarding rodent problems in their estates.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Such incidents not only result in unnecessary financial burden for vehicle owners, but more importantly, highlight broader public hygiene, health and safety concerns.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Working with the Town Council, my team and I actively monitor and work to reduce the number of rat burrows in our estate.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: We collect and analyse data regularly to implement strategies that help control and reduce the problem in each precinct.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: A municipal task force convenes regularly and reducing rat burrows is a standing agenda item.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: This structured approach helps us assess the effectiveness of measures taken and adjust our approaches for better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: However, the financial challenges of running the Town Council remain high, with significant resources already allocated to pest control efforts.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: While traditional methods, such as baiting and manual trapping provide some level of control, they may not be sufficient for long-term effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Given these challenges, there is a pressing need to explore more advanced and efficient rat control solutions.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: With more support, we can embrace more effective and environmentally friendly methods, and at the same time, comprehensively nip the rat problem in the bud.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Much of its work also involves engaging and responding to the public's tip-offs, alerts and feedback, such as in the event of water leakages, floods and canal chokes, food issues, trees falling, animal abuse and so on.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: For areas which will benefit from real-time monitoring, such as flooding, is the Ministry investing in enough equipment and resources to ensure that we have access to timely and reliable data to act on?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: One key area where technology can make a real difference in supporting MSE is in tackling everyday challenges, such as monitoring cleanliness and pest control.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: We have already seen some examples, such as in NEA's optical surveillance cameras dedicated to combat high rise littering or thermal imagery to detect smoking offences – although perhaps, not enough, per Member Louis Ng's speech earlier.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: I hope more of such technologies can be used to better protect our neighbourhoods at scale and complement the work of Town Councils.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Can the Ministry share how it intends to dial up the use of technology and AI to enable MSE's work, for example, through monitoring cleanliness in poorer performing areas, as well as tackling pigeon, urban bird and rodent issues in our neighbourhoods and, in particular, private estates, where cleaners are required to clean a network of streets which are sometimes confusing and have roadside barriers?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As we mark SG60, looking back at the last 60 years, it is not difficult to note the progress we have made since Independence.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We laid the foundations for a modern metropolis, cleaning up our waterways and environment, putting in place a modern sanitation system, reducing flood risks and improving food safety.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our hawker centres remain an important source of affordable food, a cherished social space for many Singaporeans and a proud showcase of our food heritage for friends visiting from abroad.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have also harnessed science and technology through NEWater and desalination to strengthen our water resilience and developed Project Wolbachia to fight dengue and improve public health.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The green and liveable city we enjoy today is the collective result of our boldness and our resilience over the past six decades.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Since our Independence, we have pursued economic growth in tandem with environmental protection and social inclusion.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is a careful balancing act, one that requires boldness in decision-making and the resilience to rise above our constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MSE's work is vital in safeguarding the food we eat, the water we drink, and the environment we live, work and play in.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At the core, our work is about "Our Sustainability, Our Resilience, Our Everyday." "Our Sustainability" is to steward our limited resources responsibly for future generations. "Our Resilience" is to prepare for and adapt to new challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And "Our Everyday" is to improve the daily living of Singaporeans, and our daily interaction with our environment, present and future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In this debate, we will touch on these areas.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Improving energy efficiency is critical in our drive towards net zero.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Everyone can play a part in improving our energy efficiency.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Being more energy efficient will help us conserve energy, allowing us to grow our economy and population with less energy and carbon emission.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will support households and industries in pursuing energy efficiency improvements.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For businesses, we have expanded energy efficiency grants to cover more sectors, such as construction and manufacturing sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have also enhanced regulatory frameworks for various sectors, such as the buildings and industry sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For households, the enhanced Climate Friendly Households Programme will be expanded to benefit more households and encourage wider adoption of resource efficient household products.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The public sector is also pressing ahead with its plan to improve the energy efficiency of its buildings.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Senior Minister of State Khor will share more.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ms Poh Li San asked how we intend to manage air-conditioning use.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Against the backdrop of a warmer planet, it is crucial that we manage our thermal comfort sustainably.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Very often, our indoor spaces are so cold that we need to wear sweaters in tropical Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will reduce energy cost and allow occupants to dress more appropriately for our climate.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The public sector has adopted this where possible, and we hope for partner businesses and the public to make a broader shift towards sustainable cooling.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: More details will be announced later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Under this programme, the Centre for Climate Research Singapore will collaborate with local Institutes of Higher Learning and Research Institutes to incorporate the latest scientific and technological developments; for example, in the use of AI to improve our ability to forecast better.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Just as we have risen to past challenges, we need to work together with purpose, with urgency and with determination to strengthen our climate resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I will speak about flood, coastal and heat resilience, while Senior Minister of State Khor and Senior Minister of State Koh will cover water and food resilience respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In our early days of Independence, Singapore faced frequent and widespread flooding during the monsoon seasons.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: You may recall that in January this year, Singapore experienced two monsoon surges which brought prolonged rain.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Over both monsoon surges, there was just one reported flood incident.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Later this year, upgrading works for the Sungei Serangoon Western and Eastern subsidiary drains are slated to commence, to cater for upcoming developments in the Lorong Halus area.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: That said, in land-scarce Singapore, we cannot keep expanding our drainage infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must strengthen flood resilience at the systems level, and partner building owners, developers and the wider community.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For individual developments, the Public Utilities Board (PUB) works closely with building owners and developers to implement, operate and maintain flood-protection measures.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For underground Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) stations and buildings with basements, PUB works with them to meet requirements on minimum platform and crest levels.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: PUB also engages residents and businesses in flood-prone areas and hotspots on flood risks and distributes flood protection devices to enhance flood protection for these premises.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As we enhance our inland flood resilience, we need to build coastal protection in tandem.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Members asked about the status of our coastal protection plans, legislation and standards.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To guide our plans, we are conducting site-specific studies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: More details for the Greater Southern Waterfront and Changi will be shared later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will commence the studies for Sentosa and the southwest coast by 2026.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ms Nadia Samdin also asked how we will fund our coastal protection efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Where eligible, such as for land reclamation costs, we will also use the Past Reserves.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will continue to study how best to finance these measures in a way that is fiscally sustainable and equitable across generations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is more effective to build up flood resilience at a system's level, where coastal stakeholders play their part alongside the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: PUB is developing a Code of Practice that will provide a set of design standards as well as operation and maintenance requirements for coastal protection measures.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will consult the industry this year and aim to release it by the first half of 2026.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: PUB will also launch a Flood-Resilient Developments guidebook to help building owners enhance the resilience of their premises.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The guidebook will contain case studies and a toolkit of flood-resilient measures that owners can consider adopting for their buildings.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As we experience rising temperatures, building heat resilience is a critical part of our adaptation efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ms Poh asked about our heat resilience efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are progressively rolling out infrastructural interventions to enhance heat resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are studying the effectiveness of cool coatings to other infrastructure archetypes, such as schools and hawker centres.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will find ways to improve thermal comfort for the public, such as enhancing greenery and ventilation, and reducing heat emission.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Infrastructural interventions, however, need to be complemented with individual actions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Thermal comfort is subjective and our bodies respond differently.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A key tenet of our heat resilience efforts is about empowering people.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Heat Stress Advisory was launched in 2023 to guide the public on steps to protect themselves, based on the prevailing heat stress levels.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Recognising that heat affects various groups of people differently, depending on the nature of their activities, the Heat Stress Advisory is supported by sector-specific guidelines, such as the Ministry of Manpower's revised framework to protect outdoor workers.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Underpinning these guidelines is our Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature heat stress sensor network.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will provide more accurate information so that our advisory can be more effective.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The expanded heat stress sensor network will also provide more timely information on extreme weather events, such as heatwaves.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have developed heatwave response plans for both public and sector-specific populations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked about our collaboration with partners.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We do so through platforms, such as the C40 network of about 100 cities that are looking for solutions on climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We also partner with researchers to deepen our understanding of how heat impacts our health and to co-create innovative solutions, such as developing wearables, for better heat stress monitoring.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I have touched on our efforts for flood, coastal and heat resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These are important parts of Singapore's national adaptation plan, which countries are encouraged to develop in line with international best practices.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the face of increasing yet uncertain climate risks, the national adaptation plan will serve as a long-term, living strategy for Singapore to continue thriving in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Through our ongoing and upcoming engagements, we hope to hear views from the community and stakeholders too.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The journey towards a sustainable and resilient Singapore is not just about preparing for long-term challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must not lose sight of the importance of our everyday behaviour.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This was why we designated 2024 as the Year of Public Hygiene – to highlight the importance of public hygiene and, more importantly, to harness the spirit of collective responsibility in adopting good public hygiene practices for the betterment of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We saw a 36% reduction of litter between May 2024 and December 2024 at littering hotspots, thanks to increased public education as well as enforcement efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: My Ministry also recently received the Public Toilets Taskforce's report.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have studied the taskforce's recommendations and decided to endorse them.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng will share more on this.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Hawker centres are also an important part of our everyday.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the early days, street hawkers were resettled into hawker centres to improve food hygiene standards and public health.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Hawker centres have remained an important source of affordable food and an integral part of our culture, serving as vibrant community dining rooms for Singaporeans and visitors from all walks of life.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Over time, as our people's needs evolve, our hawker centres have to be revitalised and future-ready.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With climate change, an ageing population, rapid urban redevelopments and shifting hawker profiles, patrons and hawkers have new expectations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Hawkers also require more productive and innovative solutions to meet their business aspirations and tackle operational challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As demographics shift, some hawker centres in the mature estates have experienced falling demand.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At the same time, new estates have emerged and may need more affordable eating options.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: New hawker centres will be built as needed, with modern and sustainable services and spaces.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We aim to make hawker centres more inclusive and accessible for all, including seniors and persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We also want to uplift hawker centres’ infrastructure to be ready for climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Where possible, this will be done in tandem with estate development plans, so that our hawker centres are better suited to residents’ needs, and keep pace with the times and local circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: (In English): Senior Minister of State Koh will share more later about our plans.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will face challenges that will test our adaptability – climate change, geopolitical tensions and disease outbreaks.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But our Singapore story has always been one of resilience, of a people who refuse to be daunted by our limitations, who turn challenges into opportunities and who forge ahead with boldness.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MSE's theme for the debate, "Our Sustainability, Our Resilience, Our Everyday", is not just about the policies and infrastructure, but also about our people and the everyday choices we make.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is about the businesses that embrace green investments and innovation, the households that recycle waste, the individuals who champion sustainability and the communities that look out for one another.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Every effort, no matter how small, strengthens our resilience and secures our future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Let us build on our strong foundation and press on with boldness and confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Just as past generations laid the groundwork for the green and livable Singapore we enjoy today, let us do our part to ensure that future generations will look back with pride at the choices we made.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Together, we can shape a Singapore that remains not only a thriving nation, but also a home that is sustainable, resilient and full of potential.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Chairman, recent events such as forest fires in California and heatwaves across Southeast Asia have shown that climate change demands decisive action for our sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will advance green initiatives, improve energy efficiency and promote resource resilience to progress towards our ambitious Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) to achieve net-zero by 2050.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum asked how MSE will promote sustainable practices and technologies across the public and private sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We published the second edition of the GreenGov.SG report for FY2023, which incorporates waste data and contextualises the public sector's resource footprint.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This allows us to develop targeted pathways to reduce and remove emissions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: A key strategy to reduce emissions is to improve energy efficiency across different sectors of the economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For the public sector, we have earlier announced plans to reduce our Energy Utilisation Index (EUI) by 10% by 2030 from FY2018 to FY2020 baseline.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As of FY2023, we have achieved 3.7% EUI reduction and we will do more to reach our target.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The fund will invest in worthwhile projects over the next five years, to improve energy efficiency performance of public sector facilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These projects will contribute toward our climate targets, payback through life-cycle cost-savings and generate excess savings for the Government in the long term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Eligible projects could include retrofits to energy consuming systems or installation of smart systems to optimise energy efficiency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Public sector facilities that could be covered include office premises, hospitals and MRT stations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: An example of a worthwhile project would be Tan Tock Seng Hospital's mini-chiller heat recovery system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The system saves 800,000kWh of electricity, or $240,000 a year, by replacing energy-consuming electric heaters with heat generated from the mini chiller.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The fund can facilitate the test-bedding of innovative and cost-effective solutions that could stimulate growth and help build industry capability in energy services for the built environment sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Public sector leadership in this area could catalyse energy efficiency improvements in the larger stock of private sector buildings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides reducing emissions, another key strategy is to remove residual emissions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: NEA is studying solutions to capture carbon emissions at our Waste-to-Energy (WtE) plants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are also looking to leverage Government procurement to normalise green initiatives throughout our businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: BCA and GovTech have shared the refined sustainability evaluation criteria with Government agencies for adoption in their tenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We shared last year that we planned to expand our sustainability evaluation criteria for public sector meetings, incentives, conferences, and exhibitions (MICE) tenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This will be implemented from FY2025 for Government procurement of events venues and events management services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Beyond introducing environmental sustainability evaluation criteria in tenders, we are also looking to drive green procurement in other categories, such as facility management, through incorporating broader environmental sustainability considerations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For example, JTC is working with agencies to explore incentive payments for facility management vendors who excel in energy and water efficiency in their managed assets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana and Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked how the Government can support businesses in their efforts to reduce emissions and mitigate climate impacts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As Mr Gan Thiam Poh mentioned, helping businesses to improve their energy efficiency is key to lowering business costs and improving economic competitiveness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Government has introduced support schemes, such as the Energy Efficiency Grant (EEG), to support businesses in improving energy efficiency by co-funding investments in energy-efficient equipment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We expanded the EEG in 2024 to cover more sectors, such as construction, manufacturing, maritime and data centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This has resulted in positive cost savings and sustainability outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For example, United E&P Pte Ltd, a manufacturing company, replaced their asphalt crusher with an energy-efficient model.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This change saves about $48,000 of energy costs annually and reduces lifetime carbon emissions by 1,000 tonnes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To enhance energy efficiency of our industrial sector, which is Singapore’s largest energy-consuming sector, we amended the Energy Conservation Act last year to extend Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES) for chilled water systems to existing industrial facilities.
